verses.translation_literal: A psalm of David, in his fleeing from before Absalom his son.
verses.translation_dramatic: A psalm of David. He sang it on the run, driven out from the face of Absalom, his own son.
verses.directors_commentary: The KJV leaves this line unnumbered and calls it a heading; in the Hebrew it is verse 1, which is why every verse after it is one higher than the English. Treat it as a stage direction spoken by the cast, not by David: it tells the audience where we are, on the road out of Jerusalem, in the revolt told in 2 Samuel 15–18. The Hebrew says David is fleeing 'from before' Absalom, literally from his face, the place where a king's authority meets you. The KJV's 'when he fled from' is accurate but flattens that. The word 'psalm' (mizmor) comes from a root for plucking strings, so this was a song with instruments, which is odd for a man in flight; Radak records the old puzzle of how David could weep and sing at once (Radak on Psalm 3:1), and answers that the song comes after the rescue. Play the title as grief held at arm's length.

philological_notes.note: A song sung to instruments, from the root 'to pluck, make music' (Metzudat Zion: 'from the language of zemer'). The noun heads fifty-seven psalms.
Literally 'from the face of'. The idiom of fleeing a powerful person: his face is the thing you cannot stand before.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, how many are my foes! Many are rising up against me.
verses.translation_dramatic: LORD, how they have multiplied, the ones who press me! So many. So many, standing up against me.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is built on a repeated root, rav, 'many': 'how many are my foes, many are rising'. The second word is the first said again, more quietly, as a man counting faces in the crowd and not believing the number. Keep that echo. The KJV 'how are they increased that trouble me' is fine in sense but loses the echo, and 'trouble' is soft: tzar is a narrow place, an adversary who corners you, which is exactly David's situation on the road. The word 'rising' (qamim) is the posture of rebels and accusers: they stand up. Radak reads the doubling as the surprise that his own son has turned against him (Radak on Psalm 3:2). Rashi and Metzudat David add that the 'many' may be 'great ones' (Rashi on Psalm 3:2), men of rank like Ahithophel. Say it as a complaint addressed to God by name, not a prayer yet.

philological_notes.note: 'Many', but also 'great ones'. Rashi and Metzudat David read it as men great in learning, wealth or stature; Meiri compares 'rav' in 'chief of the king' (Jer 39:13). The sense 'many' is the plain one.
From the root 'to bind, press tight'; the adversary who narrows the space around you.

verses.translation_literal: Many are saying of my soul, 'There is no deliverance for him in God.' Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Many are saying it, and saying it of my very soul: 'For him there is no rescue in God.' Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: The cruelest line in the psalm is not a threat to David's body but a verdict on his standing with God: 'of my soul' (nafshi) means about me, the whole living self. The speakers do not say God will not save him this time; they say there is no deliverance for him in God at all. The ancient hearer would take it as a theological sentence passed over a man now seen as under punishment. Rashi and Radak give the reason their traditions supply, the affair with Bathsheba (Rashi on Psalm 3:3; Radak on Psalm 3:3). The Hebrew keeps a strange old ending: yeshuʿatah, 'deliverance', with an extra -ah, which Radak says doubles the denial, no rescue in this world or the next. The KJV 'help' is too small; the word is yeshuʿah, the root of 'Joshua' and 'Jesus'. 'Selah' is an unexplained marker of a pause or a lifting of voice; do not play it as a word. The Targum renders the last words 'for ever'.

philological_notes.note: 'Of my soul', i.e. about me; Ibn Ezra and Radak take the lamed as 'about, concerning', like 'say to me, he is my brother' in Gen 20:13. The nefesh is the whole self, not a detached spirit.
An older form with the -ah ending. Radak lists it among doubled forms (compare ʿezrata) and reads it as stressing both worlds; Ibn Ezra calls it a feminine ending 'by way of elegance'.
Unexplained. Ancient and medieval opinion split: 'for ever' (the Targum, most commentators in the packet), 'truly' (Ibn Ezra), or a raising of voice from the root of 'lift up' (Radak).

verses.translation_literal: And you, YHWH, [are] a shield about me, my glory and the one who lifts up my head.
verses.translation_dramatic: But you, LORD, you are the shield wrapped around me. My glory. The hand under my chin that lifts my head.
verses.directors_commentary: The 'and' that opens the line is the hinge: against the many voices, you. Play the pivot in the breath before it. The shield is a soldier's word, and the preposition ba'ad is slippery. It can mean 'on behalf of' (KJV 'for me', YLT, Webster), 'around, about' (ASV 'about me', BBE 'round me'), 'behind' (STEPBible), and Metzudat Zion glosses it 'facing me' (Metzudat Zion on Psalm 3:4). The KJV is therefore not wrong. I prefer the spatial senses, a shield that stands between him and the crowd, because they answer the 'all around' enemies of verse 7, but an actor may play any of them. The KJV 'my glory' is correct: kavod is weight, honor, standing; Radak even reads it as the self, the soul (Radak on Psalm 3:4). A defeated king in flight has lost his honor; he went up the Mount of Olives barefoot with his head covered (2 Sam 15:30), so the closing image, God lifting his head, is exact: a man whose head has been bowed in shame. The word for 'lifts' is a participle, a continuing action, not a single event.

philological_notes.note: A small round shield or buckler carried on the arm; Metzudat Zion: refuge, like the shield that saves the one who bears it from sword or spear.

Range of senses: 'on behalf of, for me' (KJV), 'around, about me' (ASV), 'behind me' (STEPBible), 'facing me' (Metzudat Zion, kenegdi). All picture God placed between David and his enemies; 'about me' is my preferred rendering, not a correction of the KJV.
'My honor', from the root 'to be heavy'. Radak notes that kavod sometimes stands for the soul or self (Ps 16:9; 30:13); Ibn Ezra ties it to the glory that goes to the victor.

token_glosses.gloss: and the one who lifts up

verses.translation_literal: [With] my voice I call to YHWH, and he answers me from the mountain of his holiness. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: My voice goes out to the LORD, and I call, and he answers me from his holy mountain. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: 'My voice' comes first in the Hebrew, before the verb, and it is the actor's cue: this is a man who cannot fight and so lifts his voice (Ibn Ezra on Psalm 3:5). The tenses change under you. 'I call' is imperfect, a habit or a present act; 'he answers' begins with the narrative 'and', which is normally past, so the KJV 'he heard me' reads the answer as already given. Radak and Meiri take that as a prophetic past, speaking of a future rescue as if it had happened (Radak on Psalm 3:5; Meiri on Psalm 3:5). Do not decide for the audience; let the line rest between 'he answers' and 'he answered'. 'The mountain of his holiness' is more specific than the KJV 'holy hill': in the world of the psalm that is Zion, where the ark stood; and David had just sent the ark back to the city (2 Sam 15:25), so his prayer is aimed at a place he has left. Ibn Ezra notes the name predates the Jebusite threshing floor.

philological_notes.note: 'And he answers me' or 'and he answered me'. A narrative form after a present-tense 'I call'; Radak reads it as past-for-future, 'the matter is as though done, being said in the holy spirit'.
'The mountain of his holiness', Zion where the ark was (Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David); Radak offers also Moriah or heaven itself as the mountain.

verses.translation_literal: I, I lay down, and I slept; I awoke, for YHWH sustains me.
verses.translation_dramatic: I lay down. I slept. And I woke, because the LORD holds me up.
verses.directors_commentary: 'I' is stated in Hebrew though the verb already carries it, so 'I, I lay down' sets the speaker against the 'many' who were speaking in verses 2 and 3: they say, I sleep. Three short verbs in a row: lay, slept, woke. Keep them flat, like a man reporting the plainest miracle there is, that he is alive at dawn. For a fugitive with a hunting party behind him that is not small: soldiers kill in the night, as Ahithophel proposed to do (2 Sam 17:1–2). The KJV 'I laid me down' is old English for 'I lay down'; 'me' is not in the Hebrew. The last verb changes tense: 'sustains' is imperfect, a continuing hand, while the waking and sleeping are completed acts. The root samakh is to lean on or prop up, and the same root is used for a priest leaning his hand on a sacrifice: the weight rests on God. Ibn Ezra offers a second picture: the sleeper is a man in ruin, the waker a man restored.

philological_notes.note: 'And I slept', with an emphatic -ah ending (cohortative form in a past sense). The form stresses the deliberate act: I chose to sleep.
'He props me up, sustains me', from the root of leaning weight on something; the imperfect gives a continuing support. The KJV 'sustained' puts it in the past.

verses.translation_literal: I will not fear from ten-thousands of people who all around have set [themselves] against me.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will not be afraid. Not of tens of thousands, not of a people ringed around me, set against me on every side.
verses.directors_commentary: A rivabah is a myriad, ten thousand, the largest round number the Hebrew has; 'tens of thousands' is how a modern speaker should hear it, a crowd too big to count. The verse is a vow, not a report: the verb is imperfect, 'I will not fear'. The KJV 'of ten thousands of people that have set themselves' is sound, though 'set themselves' hides a difficulty: shatu, from shit, 'to place'. Metzudat David paraphrases it 'they set their faces to fight me' (Metzudat David on Psalm 3:7), and Metzudat Zion glosses it simply 'set' (Metzudat Zion on Psalm 3:7). Rashi's first reading is different: he derives it from she'iyah, 'desolation', so 'they laid waste', and gives 'set' only as a second opinion (Rashi on Psalm 3:7). Radak and Meiri read it as 'made war', and Radak adds that nearly all Israel was with Absalom except the few who left with David (Radak on Psalm 3:7). The word saviv, 'all round', paints the encirclement: he is surrounded by men, and says he will not fear. Speak it quietly; fear that is not there needs no volume.

philological_notes.note: 'Ten-thousands', the plural of a myriad, from the same root as 'many' (rav) in verse 2; the psalm keeps counting.

'They have set, placed'. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion read it as 'set (themselves in battle)', compared to 'set the ranks' (Isa 22:7) and 'set in the pride of your waves' (Job 38:11) in Radak and Meiri; Metzudat Zion compares Ps 73:9. Rashi first derives it from she'iyah, 'desolation' (Isa 24:12), 'laid waste', and offers 'set' (like samu, Exod 10:1) as a second view.

verses.translation_literal: Arise, YHWH! Save me, my God! For you have struck all my enemies [on the] jaw; the teeth of the wicked you have broken.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rise, LORD! Save me, my God! For you have struck every enemy of mine across the jaw. The teeth of the wicked, you have broken them.
verses.directors_commentary: Now the voice cracks open: after the calm of verses 5 to 7, two commands, 'Arise! Save me!' This is the war cry of the ark in the wilderness (Num 10:35), the oldest summons to God as a warrior. The reason clause 'for you have struck' is in the perfect, which may recall past rescues or announce this one as already won; Radak and Meiri take both views (Radak on Psalm 3:8; Meiri on Psalm 3:8). The KJV 'smitten upon the cheek bone' is a softened and archaic 'jaw'. The detail matters because a blow to the cheek is the standard Hebrew picture of public insult, not a wound that kills (Lam 3:30; Mic 4:14, cited by Rashi on Psalm 3:8 and Metzudat David on Psalm 3:8): the enemies are shamed, not only beaten. 'Broken teeth' is the finish: the wicked here are wild beasts, whose teeth are their strength (Rashi calls the teeth 'their might'; Radak compares Job 29:17, 'I broke the jaws of the unjust'). The KJV's 'ungodly' is churchy; the word is rasha', one who is in the wrong in a legal dispute. Say the closing clause slowly, like a man listing trophies.

philological_notes.note: 'Arise!' with a lengthened ending. A summons to God as warrior, echoing the ark's departure (Num 10:35). Radak notes the stress falls on the last syllable here.
'Jaw, cheek'. To strike the lechi is a mark of disgrace (Lam 3:30; Mic 4:14); Rashi also gives a midrashic reading, a blow to the mouth, linked to Ahithophel's hanging.
'The teeth of the wicked'. Rashi reads the teeth as the enemies' strength; Radak ties it to Job 29:17, the image of the beast whose fangs are pulled so it can no longer tear.

verses.translation_literal: To YHWH [belongs] the deliverance; upon your people [is] your blessing. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rescue belongs to the LORD. And on your people, your blessing. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: There is no verb in this verse, only two nouns set side by side: 'to YHWH, the deliverance; on your people, your blessing'. That bare shape sounds like a creed or a liturgical response, and the psalm ends on the word the crowd denied him in verse 3, yeshuʿah, deliverance. The speakers who said he had none are answered, not by argument but by a plain statement of who owns it. The KJV supplies 'belongeth' and 'is', which is fair; the ASV's 'be' turns it into a wish, which the Hebrew does not require. Note the shift from 'me' to 'your people': the man who has prayed alone for eight verses now includes the very nation that rebelled against him. Metzudat David and Malbim hear the king asking that the people not be destroyed in the war (Metzudat David on Psalm 3:9; Malbim on Psalm 3:9). Rashi reads the second half as a duty on the people: to bless and thank God (Rashi on Psalm 3:9). Close with the last 'Selah' as a held breath.

philological_notes.note: 'To YHWH the deliverance'. The definite article marks the deliverance, not any rescue; Meiri reads it as 'and not in the hand of man, not in army nor strength'.
'Your blessing', God's favor in the form of life, peace and the people's survival; Radak: that the people not die in this war.
